nameStory: The Skimming Bluet gets its name from its graceful flight behavior - it literally skims across the water's surface like a tiny blue helicopter. Unlike some damselflies that hover or dart erratically, this species has a distinctive gliding quality to its movement. The word 'bluet' comes from the French 'bleuet' meaning 'little blue one,' perfectly capturing these delicate azure jewels of our waterways.
description: The Skimming Bluet is a slender, delicate damselfly with brilliant blue coloring that seems to glow in sunlight. Males are particularly striking with their bright azure bodies marked by thin black stripes, while females can range from blue to greenish or tan. These narrow-winged insects are about 1-1.5 inches long with gossamer wings that fold back along their body when at rest. They're part of the large bluet family, which includes many similar-looking species that can challenge even experienced naturalists.

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Watch for their characteristic skimming flight just above the water surface - they glide more smoothly than other bluets, with less erratic darting movements

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Bright sky-blue body with narrow black shoulder stripes that feel smooth to the touch when gently handled - the blue has an almost metallic sheen in direct sunlight

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings fold directly back along the body when perched, unlike dragonflies whose wings spread horizontally - the wings feel papery and delicate

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely slender, needle-like abdomen that's about as thick as a toothpick - much thinner than robust dragonflies

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often perches on emergent vegetation like cattails or sedges, usually within a few feet of the water's edge where you can hear the gentle lapping of waves

habitat: Skimming Bluets prefer still or slow-moving freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, marshes, and quiet river backwaters throughout New England. Look for them around cattail marshes, lily pad areas, and shallow coves where aquatic vegetation provides both perching spots and breeding habitat. They're especially common in areas with muddy or silty bottoms where their nymphs can burrow and develop.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May and early June as water temperatures warm. Look for newly emerged individuals with soft, pale coloration that haven't yet developed their full bright blue hues.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when adults are most abundant and easily spotted. This is the best time for identification as males display their brightest blue coloration during mating season.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with some individuals persisting into September. Colors may appear slightly faded, and flight activity decreases as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts. Nymphs overwinter underwater in the mud and debris of pond bottoms, completely hidden from view.

funFact: Skimming Bluet nymphs are underwater ninjas - they can shoot out their extendable jaw (called a labium) faster than you can blink to snatch prey, extending it up to one-third of their body length in just 15 milliseconds!
confusionNotes: Skimming Bluets are easily confused with other blue damselflies, especially Familiar Bluets and Azure Bluets. The key difference is in their behavior - watch for that distinctive skimming flight pattern just above the water surface. Memory trick: 'Skimming' bluets actually skim the water, while other bluets tend to fly higher and more erratically.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bluets,' females and young males can actually appear green, tan, or even orange - the blue coloration is most pronounced in mature males. The name 'bluet' applies to the entire genus regardless of individual color variations, which can lead to confusion when identifying female specimens.
compareHints: Among New England's many bluet species, Skimming Bluets are best distinguished by behavior rather than appearance alone. While Familiar Bluets tend to fly higher and more erratically, and Azure Bluets prefer flowing water, Skimming Bluets stick close to still water surfaces with their characteristic gliding flight. Their shoulder stripes are typically narrower and cleaner-looking than those of the more common Familiar Bluet.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many bluet species, Azure Bluets stand out for their particularly vibrant blue coloration with relatively simple black banding patterns.
Familiar Bluets are distinguished from other Enallagma species primarily by their black stripe patterns on the thorax and the shape of blue markings on their abdominal segments.
Among New England's many bluet species, Stream Bluets are distinguished by their habitat preference for moving water and the blue abdominal tips on both sexes.
Among New England bluets, Orange Bluet males are unmistakable due to their orange coloration, while species like Familiar Bluet and Azure Bluet remain blue with black markings.
Among New England's many bluets, marsh bluets are distinguished by their specific habitat preferences and the particular pattern of black markings on males.
Among New England's many bluet species, Vesper Bluets are distinguished by their specific abdominal markings and habitat preferences for still waters.

Among New England's many bluet species, the New England Bluet is distinguished by its specific shoulder stripe pattern and habitat preferences, though reliable identification often requires examining microscopic details.
Among New England's many bluet species, Hagen's bluet can be distinguished by its specific abdominal marking pattern, though this requires close examination or good photographs.
Among the many New England bluets, the Slender Bluet stands out for its particularly fine, thread-like build that makes other bluets look chunky by comparison.
Among the 24 bluet species potentially found in New England, scarlet bluet is the only one with prominent red markings, making identification relatively straightforward.
Among the many New England bluets, Little Bluet stands out primarily for its diminutive size - it's consistently smaller than familiar species like Azure Bluets or Familiar Bluets.
Among the many bluets in New England, the turquoise bluet is distinguished by its greenish-blue coloration rather than the pure blues of species like the familiar bluet or azure bluet.
Among the many bluet species, Tule Bluets are distinguished by their strong association with emergent marsh vegetation and their specific thoracic markings.

Atlantic Bluets are distinguished from other Enallagma bluets by their specific black markings pattern - they typically have more extensive black on the thorax shoulders compared to Familiar Bluets, and less black on the abdomen tip than Azure Bluets.
